Assume the axiom of choice so that the library's conditional-expectation
classes are available. Let $Y$ and $Z$ be random elements and let
$\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be a sigma-algebra. We say that $Y$ and $Z$ are
**conditionally independent given $\mathcal G$**, and write
$Y\perp\!\!\!\perp Z\mid\mathcal G$, if for every pair of bounded measurable
real functions $f,g$,
$$ \mathbb E[f(Y)g(Z)\mid\mathcal G] =\mathbb E[f(Y)\mid\mathcal G]\, \mathbb E[g(Z)\mid\mathcal G]\quad\text{a.s.} $$
This is an equality of almost-everywhere classes and hence does not depend on
representatives.

For sigma-algebras $\mathcal H_1,\mathcal H_2\subseteq\mathcal F$, the notation
$\mathcal H_1\perp\!\!\!\perp\mathcal H_2\mid\mathcal G$ means the same identity
for every bounded $\mathcal H_1$-measurable $U$ and bounded
$\mathcal H_2$-measurable $V$.

The definition is symmetric. If $\mathcal G=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}$ modulo
null sets, it reduces to ordinary independence. If one side is
$\mathcal G$-measurable, conditional independence is automatic because that
factor is already known when conditioning. The choices of the zero function or
the constant-one function cause no exceptional case.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra, and $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable. A **conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$** is a real, $\mathcal G$-measurable, integrable function $Y$ such that $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. No completeness of $\mathcal G$ is assumed.

Expectation means the integral of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Integrable representatives use [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]; quotient notation is introduced after uniqueness.

Assume AC for existence. For real $X,Y\in L^1(P)$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $E[aX+bY\mid\mathcal G]=aE[X\mid\mathcal G]+bE[Y\mid\mathcal G]$. Conditional expectation is positive, preserves order and constants, satisfies $E(E[X\mid\mathcal G])=EX$, and $|E[X\mid\mathcal G]|\le E[|X|\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. Also $X<Y$ almost surely implies $E[X\mid\mathcal G]<E[Y\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Let $G=\sigma(X)$ and choose the stated version $\pi=E[R\mid G]$. By [F2], $0\le\pi\le1$ almost surely, so replacing it by $\min(1,\max(0,\pi))$ gives a $G$-measurable version with $0\le\pi\le1$ everywhere. For each nonnegative $S\in\{|Y|,Y^+,Y^-\}$, choose a $G$-measurable version $U_S$ of $E[S\mid G]$, replace it by $\max(U_S,0)$, and set it equal to zero on $\{\pi=0\}$. Positivity [F2] and $\pi>0$ almost surely show these changes are on $G$-measurable null sets, so each $U_S$ remains a version by [F1]; it is pointwise nonnegative and vanishes on $\{\pi=0\}$. On $\{\pi>0\}$ set $q_m=\min(m,1/\pi)$ and set $q_m=0$ on $\{\pi=0\}$. For fixed $m$, the bounded $G$-measurable functions $q_{m,n}=2^{-n}\lfloor 2^nq_m\rfloor$ are simple, nonnegative, and increase to $q_m$. For any such $S$, [F1] gives $E[q_{m,n}RS]=E[q_{m,n}E[RS\mid G]]$ by summing the event-integral identities over the level sets of $q_{m,n}$. Applying [L1] with $\varphi(y)=|y|$, $y^+$, or $y^-$, then using [F4] on the increasing nonnegative products as $n\to\infty$, yields $E[q_mRS]=E[q_m\pi U_S]$.

As $m\to\infty$, $q_mRS\uparrow RS/\pi$ under the stated zero convention. On $\{\pi>0\}$, $q_m\pi U_S=\min(m\pi,1)U_S\uparrow U_S$; on $\{\pi=0\}$ both sides are zero by the representative chosen in step 1.1. Thus $q_m\pi U_S\uparrow U_S$ pointwise. By [F4], the equalities in step 1.1 pass to these limits. The tower property [F3] with $H=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}$ gives $E[U_S\mid H]=E[S\mid H]$; by the defining event-integral property [F1], conditioning on this trivial sigma-algebra yields the constant unconditional expectation. Thus $E[U_S]=E[S]$, with [F5] identifying these finite expectations with their integrals. This holds for each of $S=|Y|,Y^+,Y^-$. In particular $E|RY/\pi|=E|Y|<\infty$.
Subtracting the finite identities for $Y^+$ and $Y^-$ from step 2.1 is legitimate by the absolute-integrability conclusion there. Since $Y=Y^+-Y^-$, this gives $E[RY/\pi]=E[Y]$.

citations.quote:
The **expectation** of a real random variable $X$ on a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$ is
$$\mathbb E[X]:=\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}X(\omega)w(\omega).$$
For a real constant $c$, the notation $c$ also denotes the constant random variable $\omega\mapsto c$.

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

For a parametric model with parameter set $\Theta$, an **estimand** or
**parameter target** is a specified function
$$
\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0,
$$
where $\mathcal T_0$ is a set of target values
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). This definition imposes no measurable
structure on $\Theta$ or $\mathcal T_0$ and does not require $\psi$ to determine
the full parameter value.

In a parametric model $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$,
two parameter values $\theta,\eta\in\Theta$ are **observationally
equivalent**, written $\theta\sim\eta$, if and only if
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta,
$$
that is, $P_\theta(A)=P_\eta(A)$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]). Equivalent parameter values therefore
give exactly the same sampling law. No distinctness of $\theta$ and $\eta$ is
required.

An estimand $\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal T_0$ is **identifiable** in a parametric
model $\mathsf P$ when
$$
P_\theta=P_\eta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\psi(\theta)=\psi(\eta)\qquad(\theta,\eta\in\Theta),
$$
or equivalently when $\psi$ is constant on each set of parameter values with
the same sampling law ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-observational-equivalence]], [[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).
The model is **identifiable** when its identity target
$\operatorname{id}_\Theta:\Theta\to\Theta$ is identifiable, equivalently
when $\mathsf P$ is injective.

Assume AC. Let $X$ take values in a standard-Borel space $\mathcal X$, let $Y$ be real-valued, and let $R\in\{0,1\}$ indicate response in the one-outcome full/observed-data setup of [[def-full-observed-and-missing-data]]. Suppose $P(R=1)>0$, $P(R=0)>0$, and the covariate laws overlap in this direction: for every measurable $A\subseteq\mathcal X$, $P(X\in A\mid R=1)=0$ implies $P(X\in A\mid R=0)=0$. Under the respondent law $P(\cdot\mid R=1)$, choose a conditional law $K_1(x,\cdot)$ of $Y$ given $X=x$; standard-Borel disintegration supplies such a probability kernel under AC ([[thm-disintegration-of-a-joint-law-on-standard-borel-spaces]], [[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]]). The overlap condition makes the respondent version relevant almost surely under the nonrespondent covariate law.

A **location-shift pattern-mixture sensitivity function** is a measurable $\Delta:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ for which the nonrespondent conditional law is specified by
$$K_0^\Delta(x,B)=\int_{\mathbb R}\mathbf1_B(y+\Delta(x))K_1(x,dy)$$
for every Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R$, on the covariate support of nonrespondents. This is the full conditional distribution restriction $Y\mid(X=x,R=0)\stackrel d=Y_1+\Delta(x)$ for $Y_1\sim K_1(x,\cdot)$, not merely a restriction on conditional means. For each $x$, $K_0^\Delta(x,\cdot)$ is the pushforward of $K_1(x,\cdot)$ under the measurable translation $y\mapsto y+\Delta(x)$, hence is a probability measure; its evaluations are measurable in $x$ by kernel integration because $(x,y)\mapsto\mathbf1_B(y+\Delta(x))$ is measurable ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]], [[thm-measurability-of-integration-against-a-kernel]]). The relation specifies the missing conditional law while leaving the respondent conditional law fixed. A finite mean target additionally requires integrability under the resulting full-data law; the definition alone does not assert that moment condition.

In this specified family, $\Delta=0$ gives equality of the respondent and nonrespondent conditional laws. This does not make equality of conditional means alone equivalent to MAR in a general full-data model; equality of means need not imply equality of distributions. Values where no respondents occur are outside the definition because $K_1$ is unavailable there, and a pattern with no nonrespondents requires no sensitivity function.

The formal one-outcome MCAR/MAR/MNAR taxonomy for this pair is supplied by [[def-mcar-mar-and-mnar]]. The location-shift relation above is the selected sensitivity model within that taxonomy; it does not claim that all MNAR laws are location shifts.

Fix the full-data/observed-data partition of
[[def-full-observed-and-missing-data]]. A **response mechanism** is a
specified conditional law $g(r\mid w)$ of the pattern $R$ given full data
$W=w$, represented by a probability kernel from the full-data space to the
finite pattern space
([[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]],
[[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]). In a parameterized model, write
the response kernel as $g_\psi$; it must be a probability distribution over
patterns for each full-data value.

Relative to a specified full-data law, the mechanism is **missing completely
at random (MCAR)** when, for every pattern $r$, $g(r\mid w)$ is constant in
$w$ almost surely. It is **missing at random (MAR)** when, for every pattern
$r$, there is a measurable function $h_r$ on that pattern's observed-data
space such that
$$g(r\mid w)=h_r(W_{\mathrm{obs}}(r))\quad\text{almost surely}.$$
For a family of full-data laws, the condition is required under each law with
the same response mechanism and observed-coordinate function. It is
**missing not at random (MNAR)** when MAR fails for at least one pattern, for
the declared full-data and observed-data partition. MCAR is a special case of
MAR, since a constant is a function of the observed coordinates.

These conditions concern a supplied version of the conditional law; values
off the full-data model's support do not affect the classification. This
definition does not assert that a response mechanism is empirically true or
that every joint law comes with a selected conditional kernel.

Assume the axiom of choice so that the library's conditional-expectation
classes are available. Let $Y$ and $Z$ be random elements and let
$\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be a sigma-algebra. We say that $Y$ and $Z$ are
**conditionally independent given $\mathcal G$**, and write
$Y\perp\!\!\!\perp Z\mid\mathcal G$, if for every pair of bounded measurable
real functions $f,g$,
$$ \mathbb E[f(Y)g(Z)\mid\mathcal G] =\mathbb E[f(Y)\mid\mathcal G]\, \mathbb E[g(Z)\mid\mathcal G]\quad\text{a.s.} $$
This is an equality of almost-everywhere classes and hence does not depend on
representatives.

For sigma-algebras $\mathcal H_1,\mathcal H_2\subseteq\mathcal F$, the notation
$\mathcal H_1\perp\!\!\!\perp\mathcal H_2\mid\mathcal G$ means the same identity
for every bounded $\mathcal H_1$-measurable $U$ and bounded
$\mathcal H_2$-measurable $V$.

The definition is symmetric. If $\mathcal G=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}$ modulo
null sets, it reduces to ordinary independence. If one side is
$\mathcal G$-measurable, conditional independence is automatic because that
factor is already known when conditioning. The choices of the zero function or
the constant-one function cause no exceptional case.

derivations.claim: The near-positivity law has atom weights $1/2$ at $(X,R,Y)=(0,1,0)$, $\varepsilon/2$ at $(1,1,1)$, and $(1-\varepsilon)/2$ at $(1,0,1)$. By [A1] and [F2], these are nonnegative and sum to one. Given either value $X=x$, $Y=x$ is constant, so for bounded measurable $f(R)$ and $g(Y)$, $E[f(R)g(Y)\mid X=x]=g(x)E[f(R)\mid X=x]=E[f(R)\mid X=x]E[g(Y)\mid X=x]$. Thus this construction is MAR under the assigned conditional-independence formulation [F9]. Hence $V$ equals $1/\varepsilon$ on the responding $X=1$ atom, of probability $\varepsilon/2$, and is zero on the other atoms.

For each $\theta\in\{0,1\}$, the full-data law assigns probability $1/2$ to $(X,R,Y)=(0,1,0)$ and $1/2$ to $(1,0,\theta)$. Mapping these atoms to $O=(X,R,RY)$ gives the same two observed atoms for both values of $\theta$, while [F1] gives $\psi(\theta)=E_\theta[Y]=\theta/2$. Thus the observed sampling laws agree but the estimand values are $0$ and $1/2$.

For each $\Delta\in[0,1/2]$, assign observed-pattern masses $0.3$ to $(R,Y)=(1,0)$, $0.2$ to $(1,1)$, and missing-pattern masses $0.3$ to $(0,\Delta)$, $0.2$ to $(0,1+\Delta)$. These masses sum to one by [F2]. Conditional on $R=1$, the outcome is Bernoulli$(0.4)$; conditional on $R=0$, it has the law of that Bernoulli variable translated by $\Delta$, as required by [F7]. The observed record $(R,RY)$ has masses $0.3,0.2,0.5$ at $(1,0),(1,1),(0,0)$ for every $\Delta$.

By [F1], $E[V]=(\varepsilon/2)(1/\varepsilon)=1/2$ and $E[(V-EV)^2]=(\varepsilon/2)(1/\varepsilon-1/2)^2+(1-\varepsilon/2)(1/2)^2=1/(2\varepsilon)-1/4$. This diverges as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, although $\pi(X)>0$ for each fixed $\varepsilon>0$. At $\varepsilon=0$, $\pi(1)=0$, so positivity fails on an $X$ stratum of probability $1/2$.

By [F5], the two parameters are observationally equivalent; by [F6], the different values of $\psi$ therefore show that the full-data mean is not identifiable from this observed-data model. The response probability is zero at $X=1$, exactly the stratum on which the two full-data laws differ.

By [F1], the target mean is $0.2(1)+0.3\Delta+0.2(1+\Delta)=0.4+0.5\Delta$. At $\Delta=0$ it is $0.4$, and at $\Delta=1/2$ it is $0.65$, while step 1.3 shows that the observed sampling law is unchanged. Thus the target is not identified across this sensitivity family; the interval $[0.4,0.65]$ is only the set of means induced by the stipulated $\Delta$ range and carries no repeated-sampling coverage assertion.

If $\Delta>0$, then $P(R=0\mid Y=0)=0$ whereas $P(R=0\mid Y=\Delta)=1$: both conditioning events have positive probability, and $\Delta\in(0,1/2]$ keeps $\Delta$ distinct from respondent support $\{0,1\}$. With no always-observed covariate, the missing pattern has an empty observed-coordinate vector, so [F8] requires this response probability to be constant in $Y$ for MAR; it is not, hence this member is MNAR. At $\Delta=0$, both response groups have the same Bernoulli$(0.4)$ law and $R$ is independent of $Y$, so the response probability is constant and the member is MAR.
